title: R3 Resource Roundup: Attention and Learning (Part 1)
author: Michelle Miller, Ph.D.
summary: Michelle Miller opens a two-part R3 issue on attention and learning by restating a core memory principle: we form nearly no memories in the absence of attention, so the idea that students absorb class content by osmosis while distracted is a myth. She describes Attention Matters!, an online module built with NAU colleagues that avoided an us-versus-them tone, used illusions and demonstrations instead of lectures, and let students share their own focus strategies. The module ended with behavior-change research on precommitment, the practice of setting up constraints now so that tired or tempted future-you does the right thing. She then highlights Threshold, a browser extension and mobile app built by high school students led by Jackson Brownstein, which interrupts visits to problem sites with a prompt asking why you are there and for how long. Miller values it because it foregrounds metacognition rather than raw screen-time control, and suggests assignments built around it. She previews her book The Attention Spectrum (W. W. Norton, February 2027) and a second installment with a research roundup.
points: Attention is a precondition for memory, and widespread student belief in learning by osmosis is a myth worth confronting directly with demonstrations.
Distraction advice works better when it avoids blaming students and invites them to contribute their own strategies, since digital distraction affects every age group.
Precommitment tools such as site blockers and scheduled lockouts help present-you constrain future-you, turning good intentions into durable behavior.
Threshold's pause-and-justify design shows how technology can prompt reflection about purpose instead of simply restricting minutes.
Study-skills and metacognition courses can use a tool like Threshold for reflective assignments on students' own tech-use patterns.
quotes: The attention-learning link goes well beyond keeping students from fooling around on devices in class (although that’s also an important issue, and one that we’ll come back to in a second). There’s a deeper connection to a core principle about memory, which is that we form nearly no memories in the absence of attention.

There’s no such backup tape buried in the brain, of course; the reality is that we retain only a miniscule amount of what we experience, and generally only those experiences that are juiced by a generous dose of attention.
Our position was that digital distraction affected people all across the age spectrum, and we also believed that students themselves could come up with creative solutions to the problem.
Lastly, we didn’t stop at prescribing what students should and shouldn’t do in regard to managing distractions – we ended with a module on how to make good intentions stick over time.
Essentially, present-you sets up constraints that make it easier for future-you to do the right thing, regardless of how tired, tempted, or rebellious future-you happens to be feeling.

First, it doesn’t work in all-or-nothing fashion. Instead, when you attempt to go to one of your usual-suspect sites (news, shopping, social media – the user decides) you’re directed to a page that asks you why you’re visiting and how long you intend to be there.

What strikes me about this approach – aside from the nuance – is how it foregrounds metacognition and purposeful reflection. It’s not a matter of controlling raw minutes of screen time or following rigid rules as much as bringing you back to what you’re trying to accomplish with your tech time.
